chief_complaint: finger locked in palm, failing steroid injections
hpi_details: A 77-year-old man has chronic painful catching and locking of a finger in flexion despite prior corticosteroid injections, limiting daily hand use.
ideas: He thinks the joint in his palm has developed severe bone spurs or that the tendon slipped permanently off its track.
concerns: He is worried that his hand will freeze permanently into a claw, forcing him to give up driving and woodworking.
expectations: He hopes for a referral to a hand surgeon who can make a small incision to free the caught tendon.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Trigger Finger release is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Trigger Finger release: Refer for outpatient surgical trigger finger release, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: finger locked in palm, failing steroid injections
Key HPI features: Chronic painful catching and locking persists despite corticosteroid injections and limits hand use.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Trigger Finger release.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Trigger Finger release.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing acute flexor tenosynovitis or traumatic neurovascular injury before treating as routine trigger finger.
management_principles: Plan for Trigger Finger release: Refer for outpatient surgical trigger finger release
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of finger locked in palm, failing steroid injections. HPI: A1 pulley stenosis.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Trigger Finger release.
reference_soap.assessment: Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosynovitis) refractory to corticosteroid injections.
reference_soap.plan: Refer to hand surgery to discuss outpatient A1 pulley release after failed corticosteroid injections; assess and address any diabetes or other contributing factors.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Trigger Finger
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Trigger Finger

teaching.one_liner: Plastic and reconstructive surgical case presenting with finger locked in palm, failing steroid injections.
differentials: Flexor tendon nodule from rheumatoid arthritis
red_flags: Acute severe finger pain with fusiform swelling, warmth, fever, or pain on passive extension requiring urgent assessment for flexor tenosynovitis
Acute trauma, deformity, neurovascular change, or inability to actively extend after injury requiring urgent hand evaluation

must_ask.say: How long has your finger been locking, and does it happen with every movement?
Do you feel pain or a clicking sensation when you bend or straighten the finger?
How many steroid injections have you had, and did they help at all?
Do you have diabetes or any other conditions that affect your hands?
How does the locking affect your ability to do daily tasks or work?

history.answer: My right middle finger gets stuck bent down into my palm and will not straighten out on its own. It clicks painfully whenever I try to force it open.
It started gradually about six months ago with a mild clicking, but over the past two months it has been locking up constantly.
The trouble is right at the base of my right middle finger where it meets the palm.
When I try to open my hand, the finger catches and pops with a sharp pain that reaches about five out of ten.
It is stiffest and locks most severely in the morning when I first wake up. It eases slightly after moving, but still catches all day.
Gripping tools or closing my fist tightly makes it lock right away. Warm water soothes it slightly, but I usually have to use my other hand to pry it open.
Yes, there is a small tender bump right at the crease in my palm at the base of that finger.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, there is no redness, severe swelling, or spreading warmth along the finger.
No, I do not have any numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation in my fingers.
No, I have not had any cuts, punctures, or injuries to that hand.
I had two cortisone injections in the palm over the last four months. Each shot gave relief for only two or three weeks before the locking returned.
I tried taking over-the-counter tylenol and soaking my hand in warm water, but neither stopped the finger from locking.
I do quite a bit of gardening and woodworking, so I do a lot of repetitive gripping with hand tools.
It makes everyday things frustrating, like gripping door handles, holding utensils, or using garden shears.
No, none of my other fingers, wrists, or other joints are painful or swollen.
No, the skin on my palm feels smooth and normal, without any hard cords or puckering.
No, my blood sugar and thyroid levels have always been normal on my routine checkups.
My neighbor had a similar problem and told me a small surgery released his tendon, so I wonder if I might need that operation.
I'm worried my hand is going to stay frozen like this forever, which would mean giving up my woodworking and driving.
I was hoping you could refer me to a hand surgeon who can just snip whatever is catching and release the finger.
I do not have any major chronic illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or gout.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I do not take any prescription medications, regular vitamins, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medicines, foods, or latex.
No, I have never smoked in my life.
I only have an occasional glass of beer at family gatherings, maybe once a month.
I am retired and live at home with my wife.
No one in my family has had chronic joint diseases, severe hand deformities, or autoimmune disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.6 C, SpO2 98%.
Comfortable elderly male in no acute distress, holding the right hand loosely in his lap.
No palmar erythema, puncture wounds, skin dimpling, or palpable fibrotic fascial cords.
A palpable, tender nodule over the right third metacarpophalangeal joint A1 pulley with painful catching and locking in flexion; passive extension unlocks the digit with a distinct snap.
Normal finger flexion strength in all digits; active extension of the right middle finger is restricted by locking but full upon passive release.
Intact two-point discrimination and light touch sensation across all digits of both hands.
Bilateral radial and ulnar pulses are 2+ and symmetric with capillary refill under two seconds.
